# June 23, 1956

You arrived on a Saturday in midsummer, into a world that was in the middle of shedding one set of organizing assumptions and searching, not always gracefully, for another.

---

## The Exact Day: The Plebiscite in Cairo

On June 23, 1956, Egyptians voted overwhelmingly to approve a new constitution and confirm **Gamal Abdel Nasser** as president. He was the sole candidate. The result was never in doubt. What mattered was the symbolism: a people that had lived under Ottoman rule, then British occupation, then a monarchy tied to foreign interests, formally ratifying a leader who represented — to millions across the Arab world and beyond — the proposition that formerly colonized peoples could govern themselves on their own terms.

Nasser was 38 years old. He had helped overthrow the Egyptian monarchy four years earlier, forced the last British troops out of the Suez Canal Zone the previous year, and was now the most electrifying political figure in the Middle East. He spoke to something real: the desire of postcolonial nations to chart their own course, to align with neither Washington nor Moscow, to be the subjects rather than the objects of history.

The Egypt that voted on your birthday was not simply a country having an election. It was the leading edge of a global transformation.

---

## The World Cracking at Its Seams

Four months before you were born, something remarkable had happened inside the communist world. In February 1956, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev delivered a secret speech to the 20th Congress of the Communist Party, denouncing Joseph Stalin's crimes — the purges, the terror, the cult of personality. The speech was supposed to be secret. It leaked almost immediately. The effect was like dropping a stone into still water. If Stalin, who had been venerated as a near-deity, was now officially a monster, what else might be wrong? In Poland and Hungary, the answer was already taking shape.

The world you entered in June 1956 was one in which both major power blocs were quietly beginning to fracture — and the countries between them were beginning to move.

---

## Twenty-Six Days Later: A Decision That Changed Everything

*On July 19, 1956 — twenty-six days after you were born — US Secretary of State John Foster Dulles withdrew the American offer to help finance Egypt's Aswan High Dam.*

Dulles delivered the withdrawal curtly, in a manner widely perceived as a deliberate humiliation. Nasser's response came seven days later: on July 26, 1956, he nationalized the Suez Canal.

Britain, France, and Israel coordinated a military attack in October. The United States — to the shock of its allies — refused to support them and pressured them to withdraw. The episode ended British and French pretensions to independent great-power action in the post-WWII world. The old empires had run up against the limits of their diminished strength, and an American president had made clear who set the rules now.

You were three months old when the Suez Crisis played out. You were born twenty-six days before the decision that triggered it.

---

## The Autumn You Were Too Young to Witness

The autumn of 1956 — while you were learning to focus your eyes — was one of the most concentrated seasons of twentieth-century history.

In late October, Hungary rose in revolution against Soviet rule. For a brief, extraordinary moment, it seemed as though the Iron Curtain might tear open from within. Then Soviet tanks rolled into Budapest. The West, preoccupied with Suez, did nothing. The revolution was crushed. The message was clear: the map of Europe was frozen, and it would stay frozen for another three decades.

The world in which you were born was partitioned into zones of control, and the partitions held — until you were thirty-three.

---

## The Arc

You are 70 years old, and the distance between June 23, 1956 and today is almost too large to traverse in a single thought.

You grew up in the long shadow of the Cold War, graduated high school in 1974 — the year Nixon resigned — and came of age in the 1970s, a decade of inflation, energy crises, and lowered American expectations. Men born in your year turned 18 in 1974, the year the Vietnam draft ended; you were part of the last cohort that had reason to think about it and the first that didn't have to act on that fear.

You were 33 when the Berlin Wall fell — old enough to have grown up in a world where it seemed permanent, young enough to rebuild your assumptions when it didn't. You watched the Soviet Union dissolve in 1991, the internet arrive and overtake everything in the 1990s, the post-9/11 decade reorder American life in your forties. The iPhone appeared when you were 51. COVID came at 64.

And the postcolonial arc that began with Nasser's plebiscite on your birthday — the long story of formerly colonized peoples reshaping the international order — is still unfolding. You have lived the whole middle of it.

---

## What Kind of World

June 23, 1956 was a Saturday in midsummer when a man in Cairo confirmed a power that would, within the month, redirect the course of the Middle East and accelerate the end of European empire. The world you entered was in the act of reorganizing itself — old certainties giving way, new ones not yet formed, the space between them full of both possibility and violence.

You were born into the reorganization. The world you inhabit now — seventy years on — is still working out what came next.
